title: Sixdegrees.com: A Social Media Origin Story
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (credited in transcript as "iHeart Intro" speaker for Chuck) cover SixDegrees.com, founded by Andrew Weinreich in 1997 and considered by the hosts to be the first social media site. They discuss its roughly three and a half million users, its launch during low home internet penetration and slow dial-up speeds, and its features (email-based confirmation of connections, channels, bulletin boards, daily polls). They trace its roots to Stanley Milgram and Jeffrey Travers's small-world letter experiments and the Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon game, describe the lack of photos and early digital cameras, and cover the company's shutdown in 1999, the sale of its patent to Reid Hoffman and Mark Pincus, and Weinreich's later ventures (Meet Moi, Indicative). The episode closes with a listener email from Matt, a man with autism, about impression management and being judged for his demeanor.

segments.title: Opening and SixDegrees overview
segments.summary: The hosts introduce SixDegrees.com, launched in 1997 by Andrew Weinreich, which reached about three and a half million users and is described as an early social media site.

segments.title: Timing and slow early internet
segments.summary: The hosts argue SixDegrees was ahead of its time: home internet penetration was low (about 18 percent in 1997 per the US figure cited, with Pew numbers discussed), and dial-up speeds of 56 kbps made waiting painful.

segments.title: Legacy and comparison to later social networks
segments.summary: The hosts note SixDegrees has been forgotten, with many people wrongly crediting Friendster. They compare its user count to MySpace, which reached a million monthly users in 2003, and Facebook, with over three billion users.

segments.title: Six Degrees of Separation and Milgram's small-world studies
segments.summary: The hosts connect the site's name to Stanley Milgram and Jeffrey Travers's late-1960s letter study, in which packets were passed through acquaintances to reach a target person. The study found a mean of about four to six intermediaries, with later studies on Facebook and Twitter cited.

segments.title: Kevin Bacon game and Bacon numbers
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon game and Bacon numbers, noting that several actors, including Eric Roberts, have lower connectivity numbers than Bacon. They also digress on actor Cameron Mitchell.

segments.title: How SixDegrees worked: connections and invitations
segments.summary: Users built networks by confirming connections with people they knew, inviting others by email, and tracing first, second, and third degree links. Profiles held professional and hobby information.

segments.title: Features: messaging, channels, and early community
segments.summary: The site offered in-network email, bulletin boards, and channels (special-interest groups), a precursor to Facebook groups. The hosts describe the 1999 and 2000 homepage content, including daily trivia and polls.

segments.title: Homepage engagement and early chat culture
segments.summary: The hosts recall the site showing online user counts and engagement prompts, plus a February 2000 question of the day and themed content. Chuck shares a memory of chatting online.

segments.title: Lack of photos and early digital cameras
segments.summary: Pictures were not supported because digital cameras were scarce and costly. The hosts cite the Apple QuickTake 100, the Canon PowerShot, and the 1999 Kyocera VisualPhone VP-210 as the first camera phone, and Weinreich's handling of user photo requests.

segments.title: Break and tangent
segments.summary: A break and off-topic conversation about movies, Elliott Gould, Jarmusch, and vanity license plates, with a brief mention of Weinreich's name pronunciation.

segments.title: Launch party and early growth
segments.summary: The site launched with a party in New York City for two hundred invited guests. Growth was around fifty new users a day at first, and reps recruited on college campuses.

segments.title: Shutdown and the site's domain
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the site's shutdown and that sixdegrees.com still resolves but is unreachable.

segments.title: Business failure, Weinreich's sale, and the patent
segments.summary: YouthStream Media Networks bought in at about 125 million dollars in stock, but went under because of debt financing. Weinreich's patent was sold for about 700,000 dollars to Reid Hoffman and Mark Pincus, who were Friendster investors. LinkedIn is not built on SixDegrees architecture.

segments.title: Weinreich's later ventures: Meet Moi and Indicative
segments.summary: Weinreich founded Meet Moi, a location-based dating app, whose dating side was sold to Match.com. The analytics side became Indicative, and location-based push advertising was sold to Xtify.

segments.title: Weinreich's current podcast and transition
segments.summary: The hosts mention Weinreich now hosts a podcast called Predicting Our Future and move to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: autism and impression management
segments.summary: Listener Matt, a forty-something man with autism, writes about struggling with body language, being searched at airports, and being nicknamed Terminator. The hosts respond about giving people slack.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing remarks inviting listener mail and the iHeartRadio credit.
